name: Converse–Wood-Smith otoplasty

lead: The Converse–Wood-Smith technique corrects prominent ears by building a natural-looking antihelical fold. Two parallel full-thickness incisions are cut through the ear cartilage and it is shaped with tubing sutures, so the ear sits closer to the head.
Converse described a cartilage-incision method in 1955. It belongs to the cartilage-cutting group of otoplasty methods; the reviewed material offered only animal research and general descriptions.

paras: Full-thickness cartilage incisions let the cartilage bend into a fold held by sutures. A surgeon performs it as an open ear operation.
Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting techniques carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which contributed to the growing use of suture-only methods.

angle.text: An older ear-pinning method that cuts parallel lines through the cartilage and shapes it with tubing sutures to build a natural-looking fold for prominent ears. The corrected shape is visible after healing. Suture-only methods have since become more common.

lead: The Converse-Wood-Smith technique is an ear-pinning (otoplasty) method that creates or sharpens the antihelix, the inner fold of the ear, by making two full-thickness incisions in the cartilage parallel to the desired fold and shaping it with tubing sutures [1]. People have it to bring protruding or poorly folded ears closer to the head and give them a natural contour, which changes how prominent the ears look from the front and side.

Wikipedia describes it as a refinement of the earlier Luckett approach, whose single incision produced a fold that looked sharp and unnatural, and records that Converse described a technique for lop ears in 1955 [1]. It belongs to the cartilage-cutting family of otoplasty methods, alongside suture-only approaches such as Mustarde's technique.

A 2004 report in Facial Plastic Surgery described a modified Converse technique in 210 patients with protruding ears, combining a posterior incomplete cartilage incision with permanent sutures and cavum rotation, and reported a good anterior width and a shaped antihelix and superior crus [2].

paras: Two full-thickness incisions run parallel to the desired antihelical fold, and tubing sutures shape the cartilage into the new fold [1]. Wikipedia lists the aesthetic goals of otoplasty in general: from the front the helical rim should be visible but not hidden behind the antihelix, from behind it should be straight rather than C-shaped, and from the side the contour should look soft rather than sharp [1].
The 2004 modified version used a posterior incomplete incision, permanent sutures and cavum rotation when needed [2].

Mustarde (1963) uses mattress sutures on exposed cartilage without cutting it, Furnas (1968) uses concha-mastoid sutures to reduce the angle between the concha and the mastoid, and the Merck stitch method is closed and minimally invasive [1]. Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting methods carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which has led to growing use of cartilage-sparing and suture-based methods.

Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection (including perichondritis), suture extrusion and overcorrection or an unnatural contour among otoplasty risks, and describes a soft dressing for several days followed by a headband at night for several weeks, with swelling and bruising settling within about two weeks [1].
A rabbit study compared three antihelical-fold otoplasty techniques and examined new cartilage growth and whether recurrence related to the method or to how long sutures held the fold [3].

A 2004 case series of 210 patients with protruding ears reported on a modified Converse technique combined with cavum rotation [2]. A 1994 rabbit study compared otoplasty techniques histologically [3].
